article_title: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment
citation: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Ground community needs assessment and planning in guiding principles of youth and family voice, access and equity, and alignment and coherence
description: The Roadmap to the Future initiative developed three guiding principles—Youth and Family Voice, Access and Equity, and Alignment and Coherence—alongside four shared priorities, during Phase 0 convenings. The report states these "informed the Roadmap to the Future team's work to develop the needs assessment" and will continue to guide the long-term strategic plan. Recommendations and strategic actions were filtered through these principles, and the shared priorities span quality childcare and TK–12, mental health and wellness, welcoming beacons of community life, and thriving in young adulthood.
requirements: Principles developed collaboratively with elected officials and community leaders before the assessment, and applied as filters for recommendations
constraints: Principles are specific to the Roadmap to the Future initiative's vision and phases in Yolo County
target_learners: Children, youth, and families in Yolo County, including youth in foster care, experiencing homelessness, and those who are socioeconomically disadvantaged
target_learning_goals: Healthy development and educational advantage for every child and youth in the county
examples: Phase 0 convened three virtual Children, Youth, and Family Convenings attended by over 50 elected officials and community leaders to develop the principles and shared priorities
key_sources: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673581

article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Youth-led professional development trainings on racial justice and relationship-centered practices
description: Youth-led professional development opportunities are a primary mechanism through which the RCS campaign has spread relationship-centered practice beyond its core set of actors. Interviewees from all four regions mentioned "the growing presence of youth-led trainings, which were learning opportunities that gathered practitioners and students together to learn how to better advance racial justice at school sites." These trainings were typically open to interested educators and school leaders across the district, structured by topic (including implicit bias and relationship-centered practices), and featured youth leadership, a consistent focus on racial justice, and discussion of culturally responsive and antiracist approaches.
requirements: Youth facilitators prepared through CFJ chapter leadership development
Openness of educators and school leaders to attend sessions facilitated by youth
constraints: Efforts to reach youth, leaders, and educators beyond the core set of involved actors has most often included youth-led professional development opportunities typically open to interested leaders and school staff members
target_learning_goals: Understanding how racism manifests in school structures and practices
examples: The first biannual Racial Justice, Equity, and Healing Summit, held in Oakland Unified in January 2020, offered youth-facilitated 2-hour workshops including 'An Introduction to Racial Justice, Equity, and Healing' and 'How To Be an Antiracist Educator in Oakland'
key_sources: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856

article_title: Exploring young learners’ prompted and unprompted SRL think-alouds
citation: Rebecca Pape, Joachim Thomas. (2026). Exploring young learners’ prompted and unprompted SRL think-alouds. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102294. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102294
title: Coding scheme of young learners’ metacognitive SRL activities with domain-general and task-specific sublevel categories
description: A think-aloud coding scheme for metacognitive SRL activities in lower secondary students, developed from theory and data using Bannert’s (2007) and van der Stel and Veenman’s (2014) schemes as a basis. It distinguishes four main categories — orientation, planning, evaluation, and reflection — with subcategories, and inductively derived sublevel categories separating "domain-general" from "task-specific" activities. Two trained coders independently coded 12% of participants, achieving a substantial interrater reliability (Cohen’s κ = 0.79).
requirements: Think-aloud training for learners (explanation, demonstration, and practice phases) and complementing transcripts with screen and video recordings
constraints: The inductively identified sublevel categories should be examined in other learning contexts before generalizing
target_learning_goals: measuring metacognitive SRL activities during learning
examples: The scheme was applied to 8349 coded activities from approximately 30-min learning sessions
key_sources: Rebecca Pape, Joachim Thomas. (2026). Exploring young learners’ prompted and unprompted SRL think-alouds. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102294. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102294

article_title: The Impact of Using Youtube in EFL Classroom on Enhancing EFL Students' Content Learning
citation: Alwehaibi, H. O. (2015). The Impact Of Using YouTube In EFL Classroom On Enhancing EFL Students' Content Learning. Journal of College Teaching & Learning, 12(2). https://www.cluteinstitute.com
title: YouTube-integrated lesson routine for EFL course content
description: An instructional routine in which the instructor selects short YouTube videos of approximately 10-15 minutes on the class topic, emails the URL to students two days before class, opens class with discussion and a PowerPoint outline, shows the video on a data show, then re-shows it "with frequent stops for further discussion". Students sometimes watch in pairs or small groups to complete tasks, and as homework each student finds a video of their own to present at the next meeting.
requirements: Access to YouTube and a data show in class; email distribution of video URLs before class; instructor time to pre-select appropriate videos
constraints: The article notes incorporation of YouTube "is not without its challenges", and cited literature notes poor sound quality, pronunciation and slang in some clips can make them harder to understand than traditional listening platforms
target_learners: Second-year EFL college students in a teacher-education program
target_learning_goals: Learning the theoretical content of a course on classroom observation, including observation lenses and methods of observing and recording
examples: In the study, the experimental group studied "Observation in Schools 2" content through this routine for 6 weeks, 2 hours per week, while the control group received lecture-based instruction on the same content
key_sources: Alwehaibi, H. O. (2015). The Impact Of Using YouTube In EFL Classroom On Enhancing EFL Students' Content Learning. Journal of College Teaching & Learning, 12(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1061416

article_title: The Impact of Using Youtube in EFL Classroom on Enhancing EFL Students' Content Learning
citation: Alwehaibi, H. O. (2015). The Impact Of Using YouTube In EFL Classroom On Enhancing EFL Students' Content Learning. Journal of College Teaching & Learning, 12(2). https://www.cluteinstitute.com
title: Treat YouTube as an effective instructional tool and teaching resource for EFL content learning
description: The article recommends that YouTube "should be considered as an effective instructional tool for developing content learning of EFL college students and as an important teaching resource in classrooms". It argues the question is how to incorporate YouTube rather than whether to do so, because the impact upon learning is described as too substantial to ignore. The recommendation rests on the study's post-test advantage for the YouTube-integrated group.
requirements: Instructor selection of topic-appropriate short videos, pre-class access via emailed URLs, and combination of videos with discussion and presentation rather than video alone
constraints: The article states incorporation of YouTube inside and outside the classroom is not without its challenges, though it judges the benefits outweigh the problems
target_learning_goals: Content learning of course subject matter in English as a foreign language instruction
examples: The experimental group's instruction combined YouTube videos about observing the classroom with discussion and PowerPoint presentation over 6 weeks, and outperformed the lecture-based control group on the post-test
key_sources: Alwehaibi, H. O. (2015). The Impact Of Using YouTube In EFL Classroom On Enhancing EFL Students' Content Learning. Journal of College Teaching & Learning, 12(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1061416

article_title: Youth Social Action Trials: Youth United. Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Stephen Gorard, Beng Huat See, Nadia Siddiqui, Emma Smith and Patrick White. (2016). Youth Social Action Trials: Youth United — Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Youth United school-based uniformed youth group programme
description: A programme in which the Youth United Foundation helped establish new school-based units of four uniformed youth organisations — The Scout Association, Fire Cadets, Sea Cadets and St John Ambulance — in schools in six areas of northern England. Groups met mostly weekly for around two hours, averaging 24 sessions across the academic year, delivered by trained organisation staff with adult volunteers. All groups followed "a regular structured programme of activities, working towards a kind of certification" and included a residential camp. Sessions combined theory with practical exercises such as first aid, fire safety and water sports.
requirements: Trained staff from the uniformed youth organisations to deliver sessions
Adult volunteers, including teachers, to support delivery staff
Support from senior leaders, dedicated space, school staff time, and a dedicated slot in the school day or after school
constraints: Not all four organisations were available in all six areas, so some schools were not offered the full choice
Costs varied widely by organisation, from £18 per pupil per year for St John Ambulance to £420 for Fire Cadets
target_learners: Year 9 pupils (aged 13/14) in state secondary schools in England
examples: In the trial, 663 pupils took part in uniformed group activities during the 2014/2015 academic year across 31 of 38 treatment schools
key_sources: Stephen Gorard, Beng Huat See, Nadia Siddiqui, Emma Smith and Patrick White. (2016). Youth Social Action Trials: Youth United — Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581107

article_title: The Effectiveness of Financial Literacy Instruction: The Role of Individual Development Accounts Participation and The Intensity of Instruction
citation: Radha Bhattacharya, Andrew Gill, and Denise Stanley. (2016). The Effectiveness of Financial Literacy Instruction: The Role of Individual Development Accounts Participation and the Intensity of Instruction. Journal of Financial Counseling and Planning, Volume 27, Number 1, 2016, 20–35. https://doi.org/10.1891/1052-3073.27.1.20
title: Youth IDA program with matched savings for college tuition paired with a 1-week financial fitness camp
description: A 5-year educational individual development account program run with U.S. Bank for 8th graders in three California Title I middle schools. Eligible students "save $10 a month that is matched by our program with $20 a month for 5 years," with accumulated savings transferred directly toward college tuition at an accredited college. An integral component was a 1-week financial fitness camp teaching the five Financial Fitness for Life themes plus a stock market simulation game, attended by 83 students, 59 of whom had IDAs.
requirements: Income eligibility per U.S. Department of Health and Human Services criteria; students must attend at least one financial literacy camp over the 5-year period
constraints: No withdrawals are permitted from the account; non-college-enrolling participants may withdraw only their own savings plus interest, not the match
target_learners: low-income 8th-grade students in Title I middle schools
target_learning_goals: financial knowledge, saving for postsecondary education
examples: The per-student cost of the 5-day camp was $121.47 in 2012 dollars, with about 40% of the cost from bus transportation and insurance; 93 students opened IDAs and 34 IDA holders did not attend the camp
key_sources: Radha Bhattacharya, Andrew Gill, and Denise Stanley. (2016). The Effectiveness of Financial Literacy Instruction: The Role of Individual Development Accounts Participation and the Intensity of Instruction. Journal of Financial Counseling and Planning, Volume 27, Number 1, 2016, 20–35. https://doi.org/10.1891/1052-3073.27.1.20

article_title: Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth
citation: Belentsov S.I., Gribanova V.A., Brasnik O.U., Pozdniakov A.V. (2018). Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(2): 257-264. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.2.257
title: Three-day high school youth forum with competence-targeted platforms
description: A high school Forum organized at the Taganrog institute of A. Chekhov during the experiment, lasting 3 days and involving 74 students of the institute participating in the experiment in active forms of work. Each day was constructed for acquisition of competences of civil activity through named platforms: a mass-media platform producing the youth newspaper «Grazhdanin» (communication competence), a debate platform (oratorical competence), the training course «My Choice», a propaganda-team competition (health saving competence), a discussion platform on youth policy (political competence), an intellectual game platform (linguistic competence) and a trust training course (tolerant competence). Forum work was based on stated principles including personal orientation, activity of subjects of education, integrity and systemacity, diagnostability, and humanization and selectivity.
requirements: Feedback allowing diagnosis and correction of the organized work (the diagnostability principle)
constraints: Held on one institute's platform with involvement of institute and city specialists as moderators
target_learning_goals: communication, oratorical, health saving, political, linguistic and tolerant competences of civil activity
examples: By results of the forum, organizers noted a positive relation of students to public and civil activity and an increase of level of creative civil activity of students
key_sources: Belentsov S.I., Gribanova V.A., Brasnik O.U., Pozdniakov A.V. (2018). Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(2): 257-264. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.2.257

article_title: The Use of Internet Resources and Browser-Based Virtual Worlds in Teaching Grammar
citation: Mariusz Kruk. (2012). The Use of Internet Resources and Browser-Based Virtual Worlds in Teaching Grammar. Teaching English with Technology, 14(2), 52-67. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Yoowalk browser-based virtual world used for second conditional practice
description: Yoowalk (http://www.yoowalk.com/) is a browser-based virtual world that the article describes as providing access to online virtual worlds for less resourced schools without downloading and installing software. In the study, treatment students logged on to Yoowalk, used example second conditional questions to talk to residents, and conducted a questionnaire among its residents. The article notes browser-based virtual environments offer only text-based chat communication and lack voice, unlike more sophisticated worlds such as Second Life.
requirements: A browser, and in some cases a browser plugin, since some virtual worlds of this kind may require installing one
constraints: Browser-based virtual environments offer only text-based chat communication and lack voice, one of the crucial dimensions for language teaching and learning
target_learners: senior high school foreign language learners
target_learning_goals: practicing the second conditional in interaction with virtual world residents
examples: In lesson three students were encouraged to use example second conditional questions to talk to residents; in lesson four they conducted a questionnaire among residents and answered the questions in full sentences
key_sources: Mariusz Kruk. (2012). The Use of Internet Resources and Browser-Based Virtual Worlds in Teaching Grammar. Teaching English with Technology, 14(2), 52-67. http://www.tewtjournal.org

article_title: Effect of AI-assisted caries annotation on dental students' performance in caries detection on panoramic radiographs.
citation: Pornprasertsuk-Damrongsri S, Kitisubkanchana J, Vachmanus S, Mongkolwat P, Satumanatpan P, Wiriyatanakorn P, Chatthanavej P, Boonpamee S. (2026). Effect of AI-assisted caries annotation on dental students’ performance in caries detection on panoramic radiographs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09950-w
title: YOLOv5 plus Attention U-Net AI caries annotation software for panoramic radiographs
description: A dental AI-based software that labels caries on panoramic radiographs, using "the YOLOv5 DL model ... for tooth detection, and the Attention U-Net architecture ... for caries segmentation." Trained on cropped single-tooth images split 75/25 into training and test subsets, it displays annotations in pink on the radiograph. Its training images were managed separately from the observer-performance dataset to prevent data leakage.
requirements: Trained on cropped single-tooth images rather than full panoramic radiographs.
constraints: Due to certain limitations and potential errors in the AI software, bitewing radiographs are still recommended in some cases to confirm the presence and extent of dental caries.
examples: Figure 5 illustrates a false positive at the lower left third molar and a false negative at the upper right second molar produced by the software.
key_sources: Pornprasertsuk-Damrongsri S, Kitisubkanchana J, Vachmanus S, Mongkolwat P, Satumanatpan P, Wiriyatanakorn P, Chatthanavej P, Boonpamee S. (2026). Effect of AI-assisted caries annotation on dental students’ performance in caries detection on panoramic radiographs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09950-w

article_title: Family and Individual Contexts of Middle-School Years and Educational Achievement of Youths in Middle-Aged Adulthood.
citation: Yeung Jerf W. K.; Xia Lily L. L. (2023). Family and Individual Contexts of Middle-School Years and Educational Achievement of Youths in Middle-Aged Adulthood. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20043279
title: Youth personal agency account: self-determination and expectancy-value explanations of educational development
description: The article draws on self-determination theory and expectancy value theory to explain how youths act as active agents in their own educational development. It states that "youths themselves may individually and initiatively direct and plan their own life path and development by personal agency even facing environmental challenges", and that under expectancy value theory engagement depends on one's expectancy, desire, and values placed on a goal. The account explains why educational expectations of youths showed the strongest effects on commitment, performance, and adult achievement in the study's models.
requirements: Youths must hold positive educational expectations, which the article treats as future-oriented individual resources promotive of educational development.
constraints: The article notes educational development is also influenced by family SES and parental support, so personal agency operates alongside, not instead of, family socialization contexts.
examples: The study found educational expectations of youths were significantly and substantially contributive to grade-8 academic commitment, grade-9 educational performance, and educational achievement in adulthood, with effects strongest compared to parental support and family SES.
key_sources: Yeung Jerf W. K.; Xia Lily L. L. (2023). Family and Individual Contexts of Middle-School Years and Educational Achievement of Youths in Middle-Aged Adulthood. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20043279

article_title: Innovative digital tools for new trends in teaching and assessment methods in medical and dental education.
citation: Park Jung-Chul, Kwon Hyuk-Jae Edward, Chung Chul Woon. (2021). Innovative digital tools for new trends in teaching and assessment methods in medical and dental education. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2021.18.13
title: YouTube as a medical education platform: flipped-learning videos, recommended playlists, and live-streamed surgery
description: The article describes YouTube as a learning platform where students can access content "on any device without even signing in" and are already comfortable with the interface. The author posts videos for flipped learning so students preview material before class, and algorithm-generated recommended playlists let students connect the original video with similar content from different viewpoints. The platform's basic streaming function also enables real-time interactive classes to remote students, including annually live-streamed surgery for second-year dental students.
requirements: Students must be able to access the platform; the author notes live streaming cannot evaluate students' reactions face-to-face, which video conferencing tools can offset
constraints: Live streaming's stated disadvantage is the inability to evaluate students’ reactions face-to-face, though students can communicate through comments in real time
examples: Every year the author live-streams periodontal flap surgery from the surgery site to second-year dental students as an introductory lesson
key_sources: Park Jung-Chul, Kwon Hyuk-Jae Edward, Chung Chul Woon. (2021). Innovative digital tools for new trends in teaching and assessment methods in medical and dental education. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2021.18.13
